claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A machine-learning surrogate can predict Young’s modulus for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
A machine-learning surrogate can predict yield strength for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
A machine-learning surrogate can predict toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Phase fraction, grain-boundary characteristics, and local chemical-fluctuation metrics can serve as reduced-order model inputs.
The surrogate will be trained using a blend of limited CALPHAD and first-principles data and historical mechanical-test data.
Reduced-order descriptors can adequately represent the phase distribution, defect structures, and chemical fluctuations governing room-temperature mechanical response.
Imaging and compositional analysis can provide quantitative descriptors of hierarchical phase distributions and local chemical-fluctuation patterns.
Compressing microstructural information into selected descriptors preserves the parameters controlling mechanical behavior.
The hierarchical heterostructure mediates dislocation mobility.
The hierarchical heterostructure mediates fracture behavior.
The surrogate bypasses much of the computational demand of full first-principles calculations.
Predicted Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness will have errors of approximately 5–10% relative to experiment.
The surrogate will be approximately 5–10 times more computationally efficient than full-scale ab initio and CALPHAD procedures.
Comprehensive first-principles and CALPHAD methods are computationally expensive for this prediction task.
Stand-alone machine-learning models trained on ordered compounds have limited capability for predicting fracture toughness in complex heterostructured high-entropy alloys.
Reliability will diminish when processing defects, environmental changes, or other microstructural features fall outside the descriptor and training-data domain.
Toughness predictions are expected to be less certain than predictions of elastic and plastic properties because fracture mechanisms are more complex.
The model will be falsified if errors exceed 10% for Young’s modulus or yield strength, or 15% for toughness, in a statistically significant number of blinded samples.
